topics.title: 25.1 MMU
topics.summary: The memory-management unit, or MMU, is the processor machinery involved in translation and access checking. It interprets the configured address-space structures according to architectural rules. Its implementation can include several translation caches and page-walk optimizations. The MMU does not understand a source-level vector or ownership model. It knows translation and permission information at the architecture’s supported granularity. This explains why a legal machine address can still produce undefined behavior in C or C++: the language may forbid an access that hardware page checks permit.

topics.title: 25.2 TLB
topics.summary: A translation lookaside buffer, or TLB, caches translations and associated permission information. A matching entry can supply the physical-frame relationship without a complete new walk. Real processors may have distinct instruction and data TLBs, multiple levels, and different handling for page sizes. TLB entries must be interpreted in the correct address-space context. Hardware and kernels can use address-space identifiers and other mechanisms to retain useful entries across switches without confusing one process’s mapping with another’s. Do not assume either that every switch flushes every translation or that retaining entries requires no context tagging.

topics.title: 25.3 TLB hits
topics.summary: A TLB hit occurs when a usable cached translation matches the access. The processor can then proceed with the relevant permission checks and physical-address use. This is a translation hit, not necessarily a data-cache hit. The translated data may still be absent from L1, L2, or the last-level cache. Conversely, the bytes may already exist in a data cache while translation requires additional work. A complete access model therefore tracks translation and data access as related but separate paths.

topics.title: 25.4 TLB misses
topics.summary: A TLB miss means that the required translation is not available in the consulted translation cache. The processor can search another translation level or perform a page-table walk. If the tables describe a valid permitted mapping, the translation can be installed and the access can continue without a page fault. A page fault occurs when translation or protection rules cannot complete the access as requested. It requires software handling on the reference system. The distinction is essential: TLB miss does not imply page fault , and neither event is synonymous with a data-cache miss.

topics.title: 25.5 Translation caching
topics.summary: Translation caching rewards locality in the set of pages accessed. A rough measure called TLB reach multiplies the number of usable entries by the page size, but associativity, separate structures, mixed page sizes, and access patterns can reduce the usefulness of that simple estimate. For a teaching cache with 64 entries and 4-KiB pages, nominal reach is 256 KiB. A loop touching one byte in each of 1024 different pages can have a small useful-byte working set but a large translation working set. Packing those bytes into fewer pages can improve translation locality without changing the number of logical items.

Virtual memory would be unnecessarily expensive if every load required a full uncached traversal of page tables. Translation hardware therefore caches recently useful mappings.
